rules.title: The cramfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The cramfs filesystem is a compressed, read-only filesystem intended for systems with limited memory. A cramfs image can be mounted and used without first decompressing the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling cramfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The freevxfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The freevxfs filesystem is a free implementation of the Veritas filesystem and is the primary filesystem type used on HP-UX systems.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling freevxfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfs filesystem is a hierarchical filesystem that allows Macintosh (Mac OS) volumes to be mounted on Linux.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling hfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The hfsplus kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfsplus filesystem is a hierarchical filesystem designed to succeed hfs, enabling Macintosh (Mac OS) volumes to be mounted on Linux.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling hfsplus when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The jffs2 kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The jffs2 (Journaling Flash File System 2) filesystem is a journaling filesystem designed for use on flash memory devices.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling jffs2 when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The overlayfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The overlayfs kernel module (OverlayFS) provides a union-mount filesystem that combines an upper and lower filesystem into a single unified view. It is commonly used in container environments.
rules.impact: Disabling unused OverlayFS support reduces the local attack surface. When containers or other workloads that depend on overlayfs are not required, removing the module limits exposure to filesystem-related vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The squashfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The squashfs filesystem is a compressed, read-only filesystem intended for systems with limited memory. A squashfs image can be mounted and used without first decompressing the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling squashfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The udf kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The udf filesystem implements the Universal Disk Format (ISO/IEC 13346 and ECMA-167), an open format used to store data on a wide range of media, including DVD and newer optical discs.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling udf when optical media support is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The usb-storage kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The usb-storage kernel module enables support for USB mass-storage devices, allowing portable transfer and retention of files independent of network connectivity.
rules.impact: Restricting USB storage access reduces the physical attack surface and limits a common path for malware introduction and data exfiltration via removable media.

rules.title: Unused filesystem kernel modules are not available
rules.explanation: Filesystem kernel modules extend the Linux kernel with support for additional filesystem types and related capabilities. They can be loaded dynamically to add filesystem support that is not built into the base kernel.
rules.impact: Loadable filesystem modules expand the local attack surface and can be abused on a compromised system to conceal processes or files. Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces that exposure.

rules.title: /tmp is a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is a world-writable location used for temporary storage by users and applications.
rules.impact: Mounting /tmp as a dedicated filesystem enables restrictive mount options such as noexec, reducing the risk that an attacker can stage and run executable code from /tmp. It also helps prevent hard-link based attacks against setuid programs.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /tmp and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is intended only for temporary storage, applying nosuid prevents users from introducing setuid binaries in /tmp that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is intended only for temporary storage, applying noexec reduces the risk that an attacker can execute malicious binaries staged in /tmp.

rules.title: /dev/shm is a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /dev/shm directory is a world-writable shared-memory filesystem commonly used for inter-process communication (IPC).
rules.impact: Mounting /dev/shm as a dedicated filesystem enables restrictive mount options such as noexec, nosuid, and nodev, reducing the risk that an attacker can place and run executable code in shared memory.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /dev/shm is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating special devices on /dev/shm and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /dev/shm prevents introduction of privileged programs via shared memory that could be executed by non-root users, reducing privilege-escalation risk.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /dev/shm prevents execution of programs from shared memory, reducing the risk that users introduce and run malicious software from this location.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /home
rules.explanation: The /home directory provides disk space for local user data and home directories.
rules.impact: Isolating /home on a separate partition contains user-driven disk growth and reduces the risk that resource exhaustion in /home will fill the root filesystem and disrupt overall system availability.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /home
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /home is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /home and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /home
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /home is intended for user files, applying nosuid prevents users from creating setuid binaries in /home that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var
rules.explanation: The /var directory is used by daemons and system services for dynamic and temporary data, including logs, caches, and application state. Some directories under /var may be world-writable.
rules.impact: Placing /var on a separate partition enables additional mount options and helps contain growth of variable data so it does not exhaust the root filesystem and disrupt system services.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /var and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var is intended for variable data such as logs and service state, applying nosuid prevents creation of setuid binaries under /var that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The /var/tmp directory is a world-writable location used for temporary storage by users and applications. Unlike /tmp, files in /var/tmp are expected to persist across reboots.
rules.impact: Mounting /var/tmp as a dedicated filesystem enables restrictive mount options such as noexec, nosuid, and nodev, which limit an attacker's ability to stage and execute exploits from temporary storage.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/tmp is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating special devices in /var/tmp and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var/tmp prevents introduction of setuid binaries in persistent temporary storage that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /var/tmp reduces the risk that an attacker can execute malicious binaries staged in persistent temporary storage.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log
rules.explanation: The /var/log directory stores system and application log files used for monitoring, troubleshooting, and incident investigation.
rules.impact: Isolating /var/log on a separate partition helps prevent log growth from filling the root filesystem and better preserves logging capacity during high-volume or adversarial log generation.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents creation of special devices in the log directory and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var/log prevents the log directory from hosting setuid binaries that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /var/log reduces the risk that code placed in log locations can be executed directly from the log filesystem.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The /var/log/audit directory stores audit subsystem logs used for security monitoring, compliance, and forensic investigation.
rules.impact: Isolating audit logs on a separate partition helps preserve audit records when other logging fills shared storage, supporting compliance and incident investigation.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log/audit is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev protects the integrity of the audit log location and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var/log/audit prevents the audit log directory from hosting setuid binaries, helping preserve the integrity of the audit trail.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /var/log/audit reduces the risk that the audit log directory is used to store and execute malicious code.

rules.title: Repository GPG keys are configured
rules.explanation: Repository GPG keys are used by the package manager to verify the authenticity and integrity of packages obtained from configured repositories.
rules.impact: Missing or unconfigured GPG keys increase the risk of installing forged or tampered packages from an untrusted or compromised source.

rules.title: /etc/apt/sources.list and /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ are configured correctly
rules.explanation: The /etc/apt/sources.list file and /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ directory define the package repositories used by the APT package manager for updates and software installation.
rules.impact: Misconfigured or untrusted repositories can prevent timely security updates or introduce compromised software into the system.

rules.title: The repo_gpgcheck parameter is enabled globally
rules.explanation: The repo_gpgcheck parameter, configured in the main section of /etc/dnf/dnf.conf and in individual /etc/yum.repos.d/* files, verifies the GPG signature of repository metadata (repodata).
rules.impact: Verifying repository metadata signatures before use helps ensure that repository content has not been tampered with prior to package installation.

rules.title: Package manager repositories are configured
rules.explanation: Package manager repositories define the trusted sources from which the system obtains packages, patches, and updates.
rules.impact: Misconfigured repositories may leave important patches undiscovered or allow a rogue repository to introduce compromised software.

rules.title: Weak dependencies are configured
rules.explanation: The RPM packaging specification allows hard dependencies (Requires / Provides), weak dependencies (Recommends / Supplements), and hints (Suggests / Enhances). Weak dependencies provide additional functionality that is not required for minimal operation.
rules.impact: Installing packages that are not required for the system's intended function expands the local attack surface. Restricting weak dependencies limits unnecessary installed software.

rules.title: The apparmor package is installed
rules.explanation: AppArmor provides Mandatory Access Control (MAC) that confines processes according to security profiles defining permitted file and capability access.
rules.impact: Without AppArmor, the system lacks this process-confinement layer, increasing the impact of a compromised application.

rules.title: AppArmor is enabled in the bootloader configuration
rules.explanation: AppArmor must be enabled through bootloader kernel parameters (such as apparmor=1) so that security profiles are applied from system startup.
rules.impact: If AppArmor is not enabled at boot, profiles may not load before services initialize, leaving early-running processes unconfined.

rules.title: All AppArmor profiles are in enforce or complain mode
rules.explanation: Loaded AppArmor profiles should be active in either enforce mode (policy violations are blocked) or complain mode (violations are logged). Profiles that are not applied provide no confinement.
rules.impact: An unconfined profile does not restrict the application. A compromised application without an active profile retains broad access to system resources.

rules.title: All AppArmor profiles are in enforce mode
rules.explanation: Enforce mode provides the strongest AppArmor protection: policy violations are blocked rather than only logged. This is the recommended mode for production systems.
rules.impact: In complain mode, violations are logged but not blocked. A compromised application can continue actions that violate policy, allowing an attack to proceed.

rules.title: The SELinux mode is enforcing
rules.explanation: SELinux can operate in disabled, permissive, or enforcing mode. In enforcing mode, the loaded security policy is applied and access denials are enforced across the system.
rules.impact: Disabled mode neither enforces policy nor labels persistent objects, complicating later enablement. Permissive mode logs denials but does not block unauthorized access, leaving the system without active MAC enforcement.

rules.title: No unconfined services exist
rules.explanation: Unconfined processes run in unconfined SELinux domains. Although subject to SELinux rules, those domains typically grant nearly complete access and rely primarily on discretionary access control (DAC).
rules.impact: If an unconfined process is compromised, SELinux provides little additional restriction beyond DAC. Confining services reduces the blast radius of application compromise.
rules.scope: Settings in the OS process list

rules.title: The MCS Translation service (mcstrans) is not installed
rules.explanation: The mcstransd daemon provides category-label translation information to client processes. Label translations are defined in /etc/selinux/targeted/setrans.conf.
rules.impact: Because this service is used infrequently, removing it reduces the amount of potentially vulnerable code running on the system.

rules.title: A password is set for the bootloader (GRUB)
rules.explanation: A bootloader password restricts unauthorized changes to boot entries and kernel parameters when an attacker has local or physical access to the system.
rules.impact: Without a bootloader password, an attacker can alter kernel parameters—for example to disable AppArmor or SELinux—and bypass security controls at boot.

rules.title: Permissions on bootloader configuration files are configured
rules.explanation: Bootloader configuration files define boot entries and kernel parameters. Access to these files should be restricted so that only root can modify them.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions allow a local user to change boot parameters and potentially disable security mechanisms.

rules.title: ASLR is enabled (kernel.randomize_va_space = 2)
rules.explanation: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) randomly arranges key areas of a process's address space, including the stack, heap, and shared libraries.
rules.impact: Disabled or weak ASLR makes memory layouts predictable and significantly simplifies exploitation of memory-corruption vulnerabilities.

rules.title: Kernel.yama.ptrace_scope is set to 1 or higher
rules.explanation: The kernel.yama.ptrace_scope setting restricts which processes may use ptrace to observe or control other processes, limiting unsafe cross-process debugging access.
rules.impact: Unrestricted ptrace may allow a compromised process to attach to other processes under the same user and extract credentials or sensitive memory contents.

rules.title: Core dumps are restricted
rules.explanation: Core dumps capture process memory at the time of a crash and may contain passwords, keys, and other sensitive data. Generation and storage of core files should be restricted.
rules.impact: Unrestricted core dumps increase the risk of secret disclosure when processes terminate abnormally.

rules.title: The password hashing algorithm is SHA-512
rules.explanation: Password hashing transforms passwords into fixed-length digests for storage. SHA-512 is a substantially stronger hashing algorithm than legacy options such as MD5.
rules.impact: Stronger password hashes increase the computational effort required for an attacker to recover passwords from stolen hash databases.

rules.title: Automatic error reporting is disabled
rules.explanation: Automatic error-reporting services (for example, apport) may collect and transmit diagnostic information that can include sensitive environment or application data.
rules.impact: Disabling automatic reporting reduces the risk of unintended disclosure of sensitive information to external systems.

rules.title: The kernel.kptr_restrict parameter is configured
rules.explanation: The kernel.kptr_restrict parameter controls disclosure of kernel addresses through /proc and related interfaces. Higher values replace or hash kernel pointers before they are exposed to user space.
rules.impact: Restricting kernel pointer disclosure reduces an attacker's ability to gather layout information useful for exploiting kernel vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The kernel.yama.ptrace_scope parameter is configured
rules.explanation: The ptrace system call allows one process to observe and control another, including inspecting and modifying memory and registers. The yama.ptrace_scope sysctl defines the permitted relationships for PTRACE_ATTACH.
rules.impact: If an application is compromised, unrestricted ptrace can allow an attacker to attach to other processes (for example shells, browsers, or SSH sessions) and extract additional credentials. Restricted mode limits that lateral movement.

rules.title: The kernel.randomize_va_space parameter is configured
rules.explanation: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is an exploit-mitigation technique that randomly arranges key areas of a process's virtual address space.
rules.impact: Randomizing virtual memory layouts makes reliable exploitation of memory-corruption vulnerabilities more difficult because target addresses change between executions.

rules.title: ProcessSizeMax is configured for systemd-coredump
rules.explanation: A core dump is a memory image of an executable captured when a process terminates abnormally. systemd-coredump can store these images for later analysis.
rules.impact: Core dumps may contain sensitive data from process memory. Limiting ProcessSizeMax reduces retention of large crash dumps that are typically useful only for debugging and increase disclosure risk.

rules.title: /etc/motd contains an appropriate warning banner
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd (message of the day) file presents an acceptable-use and legal-notice banner to users after successful authentication.
rules.impact: An appropriate warning banner supports user awareness and can strengthen the organization's legal position in the event of unauthorized use.

rules.title: A local login warning banner is configured in /etc/issue
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue file displays a warning banner to users before local console login.
rules.impact: A local login banner informs users of authorized-use policy before access and supports legal and awareness requirements.

rules.title: /etc/issue.net contains an appropriate warning banner
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue.net file provides a warning banner for remote login services that present a pre-authentication message.
rules.impact: A remote login banner informs remote users of authorized-use policy and supports legal and awareness requirements.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/motd are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd file should be owned by root:root with permissions that prevent unauthorized modification while allowing users to read the banner.
rules.impact: Writable motd content can be altered to mislead users or remove important security and legal notices.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/issue are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue file should be owned by root:root with permissions that prevent unauthorized modification of the local login banner.
rules.impact: Unauthorized changes to /etc/issue can remove security warnings or present misleading login messages.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/issue.net are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue.net file should be owned by root:root with permissions that prevent unauthorized modification of the remote login banner.
rules.impact: An untrusted remote banner can mislead users and weaken legal and awareness protections for remote access.

rules.title: The system-wide crypto policy disables EtM for SSH
rules.explanation: Encrypt-then-MAC (EtM) constructs ciphertext by encrypting plaintext and then appending a MAC of the encrypted data. System-wide crypto policy can disable EtM options for SSH.
rules.impact: There is an effective attack against SSH Cipher-Block-Chaining (CBC) with Encrypt-then-MAC, as described in CVE-2023-48795. Disabling EtM for SSH reduces exposure to this class of attack.

rules.title: The gdm3 package is not installed if a graphical interface is not required
rules.explanation: GDM (GNOME Display Manager) provides graphical login for GNOME-based systems. On servers that do not require a graphical environment, the gdm3 package is unnecessary.
rules.impact: Installing GDM on a server expands the installed software and service attack surface without providing required functionality.

rules.title: A GDM login banner is configured
rules.explanation: GDM can display a warning banner at graphical session login through its configuration (for example custom.conf or related profile settings).
rules.impact: Absence of a graphical login banner reduces user awareness and legal notice coverage for graphical sessions.

rules.title: Disable-user-list is enabled in GDM
rules.explanation: The disable-user-list setting in GDM configuration (for example /etc/gdm3/greeter.dconf-defaults or custom.conf) prevents display of the user list on the graphical login screen.
rules.impact: Displaying valid usernames on the login screen assists credential guessing and social-engineering attacks.

rules.title: GDM screen lock on idle is enabled
rules.explanation: Automatic screen lock in GDM/GNOME locks the graphical session after a period of inactivity.
rules.impact: Without idle lock, an unattended graphical session remains accessible to anyone with physical or local access to the workstation.

rules.title: GDM screen lock settings cannot be overridden by users
rules.explanation: Screen lock policies should be applied system-wide and locked so that individual users cannot disable or weaken them.
rules.impact: If users can disable screen lock, protections against unauthorized use of unattended sessions become ineffective.

rules.title: GDM automount is disabled
rules.explanation: Automount policies in GDM/GNOME control whether removable media are mounted automatically when attached in a graphical session.
rules.impact: Automounting removable media increases the risk of malware introduction and unintended exposure of sensitive data from external devices.

rules.title: GDM automount disablement cannot be overridden by users
rules.explanation: System-level policies that disable automounting should be locked so that users cannot re-enable automatic mounting of removable media.
rules.impact: If automount restrictions can be bypassed by users, the risk of malware spread via removable media remains.

rules.title: Autorun-never is enabled in GDM
rules.explanation: The autorun-never setting prevents automatic execution of content or scripts when external media are connected in a graphical environment.
rules.impact: Autorun increases the risk that malicious code on removable media is launched automatically when the media is attached.

rules.title: GDM autorun-never settings cannot be overridden by users
rules.explanation: System autorun-never policies should be locked so that users cannot re-enable automatic execution of media content.
rules.impact: If autorun restrictions can be reset by users, the risk of automatic malware execution from removable media remains.

rules.title: GNOME Display Manager (GDM) is removed if not required
rules.explanation: GDM is the graphical login manager for GNOME. On systems that do not require a graphical login interface, GDM is unnecessary software.
rules.impact: Removing unused GDM reduces the local attack surface associated with graphical login services.

rules.title: The GDM disable-user-list parameter is configured
rules.explanation: GNOME Display Manager (GDM) handles graphical logon on GNOME-based systems. The disable-user-list setting controls whether usernames are listed on the logon screen. dconf locks can prevent users from changing this setting.
rules.impact: Displaying the user list reveals valid account names and reduces the effort required for unauthorized logon attempts. Without locked system settings, user preferences can override security policy.

rules.title: Disable-user-list is enabled in GDM
rules.explanation: The disable-user-list option hides the list of local users on the GDM logon screen.
rules.impact: Hiding the user list makes username enumeration and credential guessing more difficult.

rules.title: GDM screen lock on idle is configured
rules.explanation: GDM/GNOME can lock the screen after a defined period of user inactivity.
rules.impact: Idle screen lock reduces the risk of unauthorized access to an unattended graphical session.

rules.title: GDM screen lock cannot be disabled by users
rules.explanation: Users should not be able to override or cancel system-enforced GDM screen lock policy.
rules.impact: Preventing user override preserves the effectiveness of idle lock protections against unauthorized local access.

rules.title: Automatic mounting of removable media in GDM is disabled
rules.explanation: GDM/GNOME automount settings control whether removable media such as USB storage are mounted automatically when attached.
rules.impact: Disabling automount reduces the risk that malicious content on removable media is exposed or executed automatically.

rules.title: GDM automount disablement cannot be overridden by users
rules.explanation: System policies that disable automounting of removable media should be locked so that users cannot re-enable the feature.
rules.impact: Locked automount policy preserves a consistent security configuration and prevents user-driven reintroduction of removable-media risks.

rules.title: Chargen services are not enabled
rules.explanation: The chargen service (Character Generator Protocol) is a legacy diagnostic service that generates a stream of characters over TCP or UDP. It may be provided via xinetd or systemd units.
rules.impact: Enabled chargen services can be abused for reflected denial-of-service attacks and expand the network attack surface without providing modern operational value.

rules.title: Daytime services are not enabled
rules.explanation: The daytime service (ports 13/TCP and 13/UDP) returns the current system time in text form. The protocol is obsolete and does not require authentication.
rules.impact: Legacy network services increase the attack surface. Unused daytime listeners provide no operational benefit on modern servers.

rules.title: Discard services are not enabled
rules.explanation: The discard service (port 9/TCP and UDP) silently discards all received data without returning a response. It is an obsolete diagnostic service.
rules.impact: Removing unnecessary network services reduces denial-of-service exposure and shrinks the system's network attack surface.

rules.title: Echo services are not enabled
rules.explanation: The echo service (port 7/TCP and UDP) returns every received byte to the sender. The protocol is obsolete and can amplify traffic.
rules.impact: Enabled echo services can be abused for reflected denial-of-service attacks.

rules.title: Legacy time services are not enabled
rules.explanation: Legacy time TCP/UDP services are obsolete time protocols distinct from modern time synchronization daemons such as chrony or ntpd.
rules.impact: Legacy time services lack modern authentication and expand the network attack surface without providing required timekeeping functionality.

rules.title: The tftp service is not enabled
rules.explanation: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) is a simple file-transfer protocol that does not support authentication. It may be provided via xinetd or systemd.
rules.impact: A running TFTP service can allow unauthorized file retrieval or disclosure of sensitive content.

rules.title: Talk services are not enabled
rules.explanation: Talk is a legacy daemon for text messaging between users on a system or network. The protocol does not support encryption.
rules.impact: Talk traffic is unencrypted and can disclose conversation content, expanding unnecessary network exposure.

rules.title: The telnet service is not installed
rules.explanation: Telnet provides remote terminal access and transmits session data, including credentials, in cleartext.
rules.impact: Use of Telnet allows interception of authentication credentials and session content on the network.

rules.title: Rsh services are not enabled
rules.explanation: The rsh family of services (including rlogin and rexec) provides legacy remote access without encryption.
rules.impact: r-services transmit credentials and session data in cleartext and provide unauthenticated or weakly authenticated remote access paths.

rules.title: The rsync daemon is not enabled if not required
rules.explanation: When run as a network daemon, rsync listens on a network port and can expose file synchronization services, often without encryption.
rules.impact: An unnecessarily exposed rsync daemon is a common source of unauthorized data access and information disclosure.

rules.title: Print server services are not in use
rules.explanation: CUPS provides printing services. On servers without printers, CUPS is unnecessary software that expands the local and network attack surface.
rules.impact: Vulnerabilities in CUPS (including CVE-2024-47076 and related issues) have enabled remote code execution. Unnecessary CUPS substantially increases risk.

rules.title: Rpcbind services are not in use
rules.explanation: rpcbind maps RPC program numbers to network ports and is commonly used by NFS and related RPC services.
rules.impact: If NFS and other RPC services are not required, disabling rpcbind reduces exposure of RPC port-mapping functionality.

rules.title: Rsync services are not in use
rules.explanation: The rsync daemon provides network file synchronization. In daemon mode without careful access controls, it can expose filesystem content remotely.
rules.impact: A misconfigured rsync daemon can allow unauthorized access to files. Historical rsync vulnerabilities have also enabled remote code execution.

rules.title: Samba file server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Samba implements SMB/CIFS file and print sharing for Windows and other clients. If Windows file-sharing is not required, Samba should not be present.
rules.impact: Samba has been subject to serious vulnerabilities and provides a large network attack surface that can facilitate lateral movement.

rules.title: SNMP services are not in use
rules.explanation: SNMP is used for network device and host management. SNMPv1/v2c rely on community strings that are not strongly protected. If SNMP monitoring is not required, the service should be removed.
rules.impact: SNMPv1/v2c with default or weak community strings can disclose system configuration and status. SNMP can also be abused for denial-of-service attacks.

rules.title: The TFTP server is not in use
rules.explanation: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) provides simple file transfer without authentication or encryption.
rules.impact: Disabling TFTP prevents unauthorized file transfer through an inherently insecure protocol.

rules.title: Web proxy services are not in use
rules.explanation: Squid and similar HTTP proxies forward web traffic on behalf of clients. If proxy functionality is not required, these services should not be installed.
rules.impact: An unauthorized proxy can bypass web filtering controls and provide a covert outbound channel for users or malware.

rules.title: Web server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Web servers such as Apache and Nginx should not run on hosts that are not intended to provide web services.
rules.impact: An unnecessary web server expands the attack surface and can disclose internal data or serve as an entry point for further compromise.

rules.title: Xinetd services are not in use
rules.explanation: xinetd is a super-server that manages legacy network services by listening on their ports and starting the corresponding daemons on demand.
rules.impact: Removing unused xinetd reduces the number of network listeners and associated vulnerabilities.

rules.title: X Window Server services are not in use
rules.explanation: An X Window Server provides graphical display services. A full graphical stack is atypical for production servers and expands installed software and network exposure.
rules.impact: X11 has a complex security model and historically has been subject to protocol-level attacks. Removing unused X services reduces attack surface and maintenance burden.

rules.title: The mail transfer agent is configured for local-only mode
rules.explanation: A mail transfer agent (MTA) such as Postfix or Sendmail should accept mail only from the local host (127.0.0.1/::1) unless the system is intentionally operating as a mail server.
rules.impact: An MTA listening on external interfaces can be abused as an open relay for spam or phishing and unnecessarily exposes mail-protocol attack surface.

rules.title: Ypserv is not enabled
rules.explanation: ypserv provides NIS (Network Information Service), a legacy centralized authentication and directory service.
rules.impact: NIS does not protect credentials in transit and is vulnerable to network-based interception and spoofing attacks.

rules.title: Ypbind is not installed
rules.explanation: ypbind is the NIS client daemon used to bind a host to an NIS domain for authentication and name service lookups.
rules.impact: NIS client software does not encrypt traffic and increases the risk of credential and directory-data disclosure.

rules.title: The rsh client is not installed
rules.explanation: The rsh client enables use of obsolete remote-shell protocols that transmit session data without encryption.
rules.impact: Presence of the rsh client increases the likelihood of cleartext remote access and credential disclosure, and can bypass SSH-oriented access policy.

rules.title: The talk client is not installed
rules.explanation: The talk client is a legacy program for interactive text messaging over the network.
rules.impact: Legacy talk protocols do not encrypt data and are susceptible to interception.

rules.title: The telnet client is not installed
rules.explanation: The Telnet client can be used to connect to remote systems using an unencrypted terminal protocol.
rules.impact: Telnet transmits usernames, passwords, and session content in cleartext, exposing credentials on the network.

rules.title: A single time synchronization daemon is in use
rules.explanation: Accurate time synchronization is required for Kerberos, TLS certificate validation, audit log correlation, and distributed systems. Exactly one NTP client daemon should provide time synchronization.
rules.impact: Conflicting or absent time sources can break Kerberos authentication, undermine log timestamp reliability, and cause TLS validation failures.

rules.title: Chrony is enabled and running
rules.explanation: When chrony is selected as the NTP client, the chrony service should be enabled at boot and actively running to maintain continuous time synchronization.
rules.impact: A non-functioning NTP client allows system clock drift, which can break PKI validation, Kerberos authentication, and correlation of security events.

rules.title: The cron daemon is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The cron daemon executes scheduled jobs, including system maintenance, log rotation, and security-related tasks.
rules.impact: A non-functioning cron service can cause missed maintenance tasks such as log rotation, integrity checks, and scheduled security updates.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/crontab are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/crontab file defines system-wide scheduled jobs. Restrictive permissions and root ownership prevent unauthorized reading or modification of the schedule.
rules.impact: Write access to /etc/crontab allows insertion of jobs that run with elevated privileges, a common persistence technique.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.hourly are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.hourly directory contains scripts executed hourly with root privileges. Restrictive ownership and permissions prevent unauthorized job placement.
rules.impact: Write access to /etc/cron.hourly allows an attacker to place a script that runs hourly as root, enabling persistence and privilege abuse.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.daily are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.daily directory contains scripts executed daily with root privileges. Restrictive permissions prevent unauthorized addition of malicious jobs.
rules.impact: Compromise of /etc/cron.daily allows arbitrary code to run daily as root, providing persistent privileged access.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.weekly are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.weekly directory contains weekly maintenance scripts executed as root. Correct permissions prevent injection of unauthorized jobs.
rules.impact: An unauthorized script in /etc/cron.weekly executes with root privileges on a weekly schedule, which can make malicious jobs harder to notice.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.monthly are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.monthly directory contains monthly jobs executed as root. Restrictive permissions are required for all cron directories that run privileged scripts.
rules.impact: A malicious monthly cron job can run with full root privileges on an infrequent schedule that is easy to overlook during routine monitoring.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.d are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.d directory contains drop-in cron schedule files. Restrictive permissions and root ownership prevent unauthorized job definitions.
rules.impact: Write access to /etc/cron.d allows creation of named cron files with arbitrary schedules and root-executed commands.

rules.title: Crontab is restricted to authorized users
rules.explanation: Access to user crontab can be controlled with /etc/cron.allow (allowlist) rather than /etc/cron.deny. Only explicitly authorized users should be permitted to create user cron jobs.
rules.impact: Without crontab restrictions, any local user can schedule recurring commands, increasing the impact of account compromise and complicating monitoring.

rules.title: Crontab access is configured
rules.explanation: Access to the crontab command for managing user scheduled jobs should be configured so that only authorized users can create or modify personal cron entries.
rules.impact: Restricting crontab access prevents unauthorized creation or modification of scheduled jobs by unprivileged users.

rules.title: At is restricted to authorized users
rules.explanation: The at utility schedules one-time command execution. Access should be restricted using /etc/at.allow as an allowlist rather than relying solely on /etc/at.deny.
rules.impact: Without at restrictions, any user can schedule deferred execution of arbitrary commands, increasing the impact of a compromised account.

rules.title: Access to systemd timer unit files is configured
rules.explanation: Systemd timer unit files define scheduled timer-based jobs. Permissions on these files should restrict unauthorized modification of system scheduling configuration.
rules.impact: Writable timer unit files allow creation or alteration of scheduled tasks that may run with elevated privileges.

rules.title: Access to systemd service unit files is configured
rules.explanation: Systemd service unit files define how services are started and managed. Permissions on these files should prevent unauthorized modification of service definitions.
rules.impact: Writable service unit files allow an attacker to alter service startup behavior or inject malicious commands into privileged services.

rules.title: Access to systemd timer drop-in directories is configured
rules.explanation: Systemd timer drop-in directories hold override fragments for timer units. Access to these directories should be restricted to prevent unauthorized scheduling changes.
rules.impact: Writable timer drop-in directories allow insertion of override fragments that can alter or add privileged scheduled tasks.
rules.scope: Settings in systemd timer drop-in directories

rules.title: Systemd user timers disable-linger is configured
rules.explanation: Systemd user lingering controls whether user services and timers continue after logout. disable-linger configuration prevents unintended persistence of user-scoped timers.
rules.impact: Allowing linger without policy control can leave user timers running after logout, expanding persistence opportunities for compromised accounts.

rules.title: ICMP redirects are not sent
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects parameter controls whether the system may send ICMP Redirect messages that instruct other hosts to use an alternate route.
rules.impact: Sending ICMP redirects from a non-router host can allow a compromised system to influence routing decisions and redirect traffic.

rules.title: IP forwarding is disabled
rules.explanation: IP forwarding (net.ipv4.ip_forward and net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding) determines whether the system routes packets between network interfaces.
rules.impact: Enabled forwarding on a non-router host can permit cross-network traffic flows and facilitate man-in-the-middle attacks.

rules.title: Bluetooth services are disabled
rules.explanation: Bluetooth provides short-range wireless connectivity for peripherals and data transfer. On many servers it is unused.
rules.impact: Disabling unused Bluetooth reduces the wireless and driver attack surface.

rules.title: Source-routed packets are not accepted
rules.explanation: Source routing allows a packet sender to specify the path a packet takes through the network. The accept_source_route settings control whether such packets are accepted for IPv4 and IPv6.
rules.impact: Accepting source-routed packets can allow attackers to bypass normal routing and filtering controls.

rules.title: ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: ICMP Redirect messages instruct a host to send traffic via an alternate gateway. The accept_redirects settings control whether such messages are accepted for IPv4 and IPv6.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP redirects can allow an attacker to manipulate host routing and intercept traffic.

rules.title: Secure ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are redirect messages that appear to come from a gateway listed in the system's default gateway list. Even these should typically be rejected on non-router hosts.
rules.impact: Accepting secure redirects still permits route manipulation if a known gateway is compromised or spoofed.

rules.title: Suspicious packets are logged
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians setting causes the kernel to log packets with impossible or non-routable source addresses (martian packets).
rules.impact: Without martian logging, administrators have reduced visibility into spoofing and routing anomalies that may indicate attack activity.

rules.title: Broadcast ICMP requests are ignored
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts setting causes the system to ignore ICMP echo requests sent to broadcast or multicast addresses.
rules.impact: Responding to broadcast ICMP echo requests can allow the host to participate in Smurf-style denial-of-service amplification attacks.

rules.title: Bogus ICMP responses are ignored
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses setting controls whether the kernel ignores ICMP error responses that do not comply with RFC 1122.
rules.impact: Processing bogus ICMP responses can generate noisy logs and, in some cases, disrupt normal network communication.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.ip_forward parameter is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.ip_forward flag indicates whether the system may forward IPv4 packets between interfaces.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.ip_forward to 0 on a non-router host prevents the system from routing IPv4 traffic between interfaces and reduces unintended network exposure.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding parameter is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding parameter controls IPv4 packet forwarding on all network interfaces.
rules.impact: Disabling forwarding on non-router hosts prevents the system from routing traffic between interfaces and reduces unnecessary advertisement of routing capability.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding parameter is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding parameter controls IPv4 packet forwarding on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Configuring the default forwarding setting ensures newly added interfaces do not unexpectedly begin routing traffic on non-router hosts.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects parameter is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP Redirects are used to send routing information to other hosts. On a host-only system that is not acting as a router, sending redirects is unnecessary. net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects controls sending of IPv4 ICMP redirects on all interfaces.
rules.impact: An attacker can use a compromised host to send invalid ICMP redirects that disrupt routing and direct users to attacker-controlled systems.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP Redirects convey routing information to other hosts. On a host-only system, sending redirects is unnecessary. net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects controls sending of IPv4 ICMP redirects on newly added interfaces.
rules.impact: An attacker can use a compromised host to send invalid ICMP redirects that disrupt routing and direct users to attacker-controlled systems.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses parameter is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses controls whether the kernel logs ICMP error responses from broadcast frames that do not comply with RFC 1122.
rules.impact: Some routers and attackers send non-compliant ICMP replies that can flood logs with useless error messages and obscure genuine security events.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts controls whether ICMP echo and timestamp requests addressed to broadcast or multicast destinations are ignored.
rules.impact: Accepting broadcast or multicast ICMP echo requests can allow the host to participate in Smurf amplification attacks that generate large volumes of reply traffic toward a spoofed victim.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects parameter is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP redirect messages convey routing information and can instruct a host to send packets via an alternate path. net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects controls acceptance of IPv4 ICMP redirects on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Setting accept_redirects to 0 prevents outsiders from updating the system's IPv4 routing tables through ICMP redirect messages.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP redirect messages can instruct a host to send packets via an alternate path. net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects controls acceptance of IPv4 ICMP redirects on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Configuring the default setting prevents newly added interfaces from accepting IPv4 ICMP redirects that could alter host routing.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects parameter is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are similar to ordinary redirects except they purport to come from gateways listed in the default gateway list.
rules.impact: Even known gateways can be compromised. Setting secure_redirects to 0 prevents IPv4 routing-table updates from potentially untrustworthy gateway redirects.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects purport to come from gateways listed in the default gateway list. net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects applies this control to newly added interfaces.
rules.impact: Disabling secure redirects on new interfaces prevents potentially compromised gateways from updating IPv4 routing tables on those interfaces.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter parameter is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter enables reverse-path filtering for IPv4 traffic on all interfaces. When enabled, packets are dropped if the source address is not reachable via the interface on which they arrived.
rules.impact: Reverse-path filtering helps deter IP spoofing. Note that asymmetric routing (for example with dynamic routing protocols) may be incompatible with strict reverse-path filtering.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter enables reverse-path filtering for IPv4 traffic on newly added interfaces, dropping packets whose source address is not reachable via the arrival interface.
rules.impact: Configuring the default reverse-path filter helps deter spoofed packets on new interfaces, with the same asymmetric-routing caveats as the all-interfaces setting.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: The accept_source_route parameter causes interfaces to accept packets with Strict Source Route (SSR) or Loose Source Routing (LSR) options. net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route applies this control to all IPv4 interfaces.
rules.impact: Disabling source routing prevents attackers from specifying packet paths that bypass ordinary routing restrictions between public and private networks.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route parameter is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route controls acceptance of IPv4 packets with SSR or LSR source-routing options on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Disabling source routing on new interfaces prevents attackers from using source-routed packets to reach otherwise unreachable private addresses.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians is configured
rules.explanation: When enabled, log_martians records packets with non-routable source addresses in the kernel log. net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians applies this logging on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Logging martian packets helps administrators investigate possible spoofing activity directed at the system.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians parameter is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians controls whether IPv4 packets with non-routable source addresses are logged for newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Enabling martian logging on new interfaces improves visibility into spoofed or malformed traffic arriving on those interfaces.

rules.title: The net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies parameter is configured
rules.explanation: When tcp_syncookies is enabled, the kernel can continue accepting valid TCP connections under SYN flood conditions by encoding connection state in SYN/ACK sequence numbers instead of consuming half-open queue slots.
rules.impact: SYN flood attacks exhaust the half-open connection queue and deny service to legitimate clients. SYN cookies allow valid connections to continue during such attacks.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.lo.route_localnet is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.conf.lo.route_localnet parameter controls whether the loopback interface may route traffic destined for 127/8 addresses received from other interfaces.
rules.impact: Misconfiguration of route_localnet can expose loopback-only services to remote access and increase the local network attack surface.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding parameter is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding flag indicates whether the system may forward IPv6 packets between interfaces.
rules.impact: Setting IPv6 forwarding to 0 on a non-router host prevents the system from routing IPv6 traffic between interfaces.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding parameter is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding parameter controls whether newly added interfaces forward IPv6 packets.
rules.impact: Configuring the default IPv6 forwarding setting prevents newly added interfaces from unexpectedly routing IPv6 traffic on non-router hosts.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects parameter is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP redirect messages can instruct a host to send packets via an alternate path. net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects controls acceptance of IPv6 ICMP redirects on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Rejecting IPv6 ICMP redirects prevents outsiders from updating the system's IPv6 routing tables through redirect messages.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects controls acceptance of IPv6 ICMP redirect messages on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Configuring the default setting prevents newly added interfaces from accepting IPv6 redirects that could alter host routing.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route controls acceptance of IPv6 packets with Strict Source Route (SSR) or Loose Source Routing (LSR) options on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Disabling IPv6 source routing prevents attackers from specifying packet paths that bypass ordinary routing restrictions.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route parameter is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route controls acceptance of IPv6 source-routed packets on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Disabling source routing on new interfaces prevents use of source-routed IPv6 packets to reach otherwise unreachable networks.

rules.title: The net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra parameter is configured
rules.explanation: Routers periodically send multicast Router Advertisement (RA) messages to announce availability and autoconfiguration information. net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra controls acceptance of IPv6 RA messages on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Accepting rogue router advertisements can cause the system to route traffic through compromised machines. Preferring static trusted routes reduces this risk.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra controls acceptance of IPv6 Router Advertisement messages on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Rejecting router advertisements on new interfaces helps prevent autoconfiguration of routes toward untrusted or compromised gateways.

rules.title: The auditd service is installed and running
rules.explanation: The auditd package provides the Linux audit daemon, which records security-relevant user actions and system events for monitoring and incident investigation.
rules.impact: Without auditing, administrators have limited ability to identify attack activity and security policy violations after the fact.

rules.title: Auditd is enabled at boot
rules.explanation: The auditd service should be enabled so that it starts automatically at boot and records events from system startup.
rules.impact: If auditd is not enabled at boot, a logging gap exists during early system operation when critical events may occur.

rules.title: Audit=1 is set in the bootloader configuration
rules.explanation: The audit=1 kernel parameter enables auditing early in the boot process so that events occurring before auditd starts are not lost. It is typically set in GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub.
rules.impact: Without early auditing, actions that occur before the audit daemon starts cannot be reconstructed from the audit trail.

rules.title: Audit_backlog_limit is sufficient
rules.explanation: The audit_backlog_limit kernel parameter defines the size of the audit event buffer during early boot, before auditd is available. A value of at least 8192 is commonly required.
rules.impact: An insufficient backlog causes loss of early-boot audit events under load, creating gaps in the security audit trail.

rules.title: Max_log_file is configured in auditd.conf
rules.explanation: The max_log_file setting in /etc/audit/auditd.conf defines the maximum size of an individual audit log file before rotation or other configured actions occur.
rules.impact: Without log size limits, audit logs can grow without bound and exhaust disk space on the audit or /var filesystem.

rules.title: Max_log_file_action is not set to delete
rules.explanation: The max_log_file_action setting controls what auditd does when a log file reaches its maximum size. Automatic deletion of audit logs should not be used.
rules.impact: Deleting audit logs destroys evidence needed for incident investigation and compliance.

rules.title: Space_left_action is configured appropriately
rules.explanation: The space_left_action setting in /etc/audit/auditd.conf defines the system response when free space on the audit log partition falls to a configured threshold. Halt or single-user responses preserve audit integrity.
rules.impact: Ignoring audit disk exhaustion can result in loss of audit data and allow attacks to proceed without a complete trail.

rules.title: Password quality requirements are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/pwquality.conf file defines minimum password length and character-class requirements such as uppercase, lowercase, digits, and other characters.
rules.impact: Weak password quality requirements make passwords easier to guess or crack, increasing the likelihood of account compromise.

rules.title: Account lockout is configured in faillock.conf
rules.explanation: The faillock mechanism locks an account after a configured number of consecutive failed authentication attempts for a defined unlock interval (for example deny 5 and unlock_time 900).
rules.impact: Without failed-attempt lockout, online password brute-force attacks against local accounts are substantially easier.

rules.title: ENCRYPT_METHOD is set to SHA512
rules.explanation: ENCRYPT_METHOD in /etc/login.defs (and related PAM configuration) selects the password hashing algorithm used for new and changed passwords. SHA-512 provides strong protection relative to legacy algorithms.
rules.impact: Legacy methods such as MD5 or DES provide weak password protection and allow faster offline cracking if hashes are obtained.

rules.title: SSH access is restricted
rules.explanation: The AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, or DenyGroups directives in SSH configuration restrict which users and groups may authenticate remotely. This implements least privilege for remote logon.
rules.impact: Without explicit access restrictions, all accounts—including service accounts—may have SSH access. Compromise of any such account provides a remote entry point.

rules.title: The SSH banner is configured
rules.explanation: The SSH Banner directive displays a warning message to clients before authentication completes.
rules.impact: A legal warning banner before authentication supports awareness and may assist legal proceedings related to unauthorized access.

rules.title: SSH ciphers are configured
rules.explanation: The SSH Ciphers directive specifies the symmetric encryption algorithms permitted for SSH sessions.
rules.impact: Restricting SSH to modern, strong ciphers reduces exposure to weak or obsolete encryption algorithms.

rules.title: SSH ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
rules.explanation: ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax control how SSH detects and terminates idle or unresponsive client sessions.
rules.impact: Proper keepalive limits reduce the lifetime of abandoned sessions that could be hijacked and free server resources held by stale connections.

rules.title: SSH DisableForwarding is enabled
rules.explanation: The DisableForwarding directive disables SSH TCP and X11 forwarding features that can tunnel arbitrary network traffic through an SSH session.
rules.impact: Disabling forwarding reduces the risk that SSH is used to bypass network segmentation and access controls.

rules.title: SSH GSSAPIAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: GSSAPIAuthentication enables SSH authentication via GSSAPI mechanisms such as Kerberos. When unused, it adds complexity and optional attack surface.
rules.impact: Disabling unused GSSAPI authentication simplifies the SSH authentication path and removes an unnecessary dependency.

rules.title: SSH HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: HostbasedAuthentication trusts the remote host identity rather than verifying the individual user. It is a legacy method superseded by public-key and other stronger authentication options.
rules.impact: Host-based authentication can allow passwordless access from trusted hosts. Compromise of any trusted host can yield immediate access without further user authentication.

rules.title: SSH IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter disables use of .rhosts and .shosts files for SSH authentication. These are obsolete, host-trust mechanisms.
rules.impact: .rhosts-style trust can permit logon from a listed host without a password. IP spoofing or compromise of a trusted host can yield unauthenticated access.

rules.title: SSH KexAlgorithms are configured
rules.explanation: The KexAlgorithms directive specifies the key-exchange algorithms permitted during SSH session setup.
rules.impact: Restricting key exchange to modern, secure algorithms reduces exposure to weak cryptographic negotiation.

rules.title: The SSH LoginGraceTime parameter is configured
rules.explanation: LoginGraceTime defines how long an unauthenticated SSH connection may remain open while authentication is attempted. A modest value (for example 30–60 seconds) limits resource consumption by incomplete connections.
rules.impact: A large or unlimited LoginGraceTime allows attackers to hold many incomplete connections, contributing to denial of service and prolonging slow guessing attacks.

rules.title: The SSH logging level is configured
rules.explanation: The SSH LogLevel setting (typically VERBOSE or INFO) controls the detail recorded for authentication and session events.
rules.impact: Insufficient SSH logging reduces the ability to detect password-guessing attacks, unauthorized logons, and anomalous remote activity.

rules.title: SSH MAC algorithms are configured
rules.explanation: Message authentication code (MAC) algorithms protect the integrity of SSH traffic. Obsolete algorithms such as HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA1 are weaker and should be excluded.
rules.impact: Weak MAC algorithms increase the risk that an on-path attacker can modify SSH packets without detection.

rules.title: The SSH MaxAuthTries parameter is configured
rules.explanation: MaxAuthTries limits the number of authentication attempts permitted per SSH connection. A low value (for example no more than 4) constrains guessing within a single session.
rules.impact: Without an authentication-attempt limit, an attacker can perform extensive password guessing within one connection, accelerating brute-force attacks.

rules.title: The SSH MaxSessions parameter is configured
rules.explanation: MaxSessions limits the number of multiplexed sessions that may be opened over a single SSH connection.
rules.impact: Unlimited sessions over one connection can contribute to denial of service and make auditing of active sessions more difficult.

rules.title: The SSH MaxStartups parameter is configured
rules.explanation: MaxStartups limits the number of concurrent unauthenticated incoming SSH connections the daemon will accept.
rules.impact: Without MaxStartups limits, an attacker can open large numbers of incomplete connections and deny SSH access to legitimate administrators.

rules.title: SSH login with empty passwords is disabled
rules.explanation: Disallowing empty passwords ensures that accounts without a password cannot authenticate via SSH.
rules.impact: Allowing empty passwords means accounts with no password set may be accessible via SSH without authentication.

rules.title: SSH root login is disabled
rules.explanation: Disallowing direct SSH login as root requires administrators to authenticate with individual accounts and elevate privileges through controlled mechanisms such as sudo.
rules.impact: Permitting root SSH login means successful credential theft or brute force immediately yields full system control, and audit trails cannot distinguish among administrators.

rules.title: SSH PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitUserEnvironment allows users to set environment variables through ~/.ssh/environment and similar mechanisms during session setup.
rules.impact: User-controlled environment files can set variables such as LD_PRELOAD or PATH to bypass restrictions and execute unintended code.

rules.title: SSH UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: UsePAM enables the Pluggable Authentication Modules interface for SSH, allowing centralized password policy, account lockout, and session handling to apply to SSH logons.
rules.impact: Without UsePAM, SSH may bypass PAM controls such as pam_faillock, password quality enforcement, and MFA integrations, weakening authentication security.

rules.title: SSH UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: UsePAM enables the Pluggable Authentication Modules interface for SSH, allowing centralized password policy, account lockout, and session handling to apply to SSH logons.
rules.impact: Without UsePAM, SSH may bypass PAM controls such as pam_faillock, password quality enforcement, and MFA integrations, weakening authentication security.

rules.title: Sshd ListenAddress is configured
rules.explanation: The ListenAddress directive restricts the network addresses on which the SSH daemon accepts connections.
rules.impact: Binding SSH only to required addresses reduces exposure of the remote administration service on unintended interfaces.

rules.title: Root login is restricted to authorized terminals
rules.explanation: The /etc/securetty file lists terminals on which root may log in directly. It should contain only approved console devices.
rules.impact: Unrestricted root login terminals increase opportunities for unauthorized privileged access.

rules.title: Pam_wheel is enabled to restrict su
rules.explanation: The pam_wheel module in /etc/pam.d/su restricts use of the su command to members of a designated group such as wheel or sudo.
rules.impact: Unrestricted su access increases the risk that any local user can attempt password-based elevation to root.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH host public key files are configured
rules.explanation: SSH host public key files identify the server to clients and are used to verify signatures associated with the corresponding host private key.
rules.impact: If host public key files can be modified by unauthorized users, trust in the SSH service identity can be undermined.

rules.title: Users must authenticate to elevate privileges
rules.explanation: NOPASSWD entries in sudoers disable the password requirement when executing privileged commands. Such entries remove an important confirmation step for privilege elevation.
rules.impact: Without a password requirement, compromise of a user session or SSH key can immediately yield root privileges with no additional barrier.

rules.title: Re-authentication for privilege elevation is not disabled globally
rules.explanation: A global !authenticate flag in sudoers disables authentication for sudo across users, undermining sudo's primary access-control mechanism.
rules.impact: Globally disabling sudo authentication allows privileged command execution without password confirmation, so capture of any authorized user session can lead to full compromise.

rules.title: SSH PAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the PAM interface for SSH. When enabled, PAM can handle authentication, account, and session processing in conjunction with SSH password and challenge-response settings.
rules.impact: PAM integration allows account restrictions, session environment controls, and complementary authentication factors to apply consistently to SSH access.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a shell or command as another user. Enabling pam_wheel.so in /etc/pam.d/su restricts su to members of a designated group, reinforcing use of sudo for controlled privilege elevation.
rules.impact: Restricting su and preferring sudo improves control over privilege elevation and provides richer command auditing than su alone.
rules.scope: Settings in /etc/pam.d/su: pam_wheel.so, and group in /etc/group

rules.title: Lockout for failed login attempts is configured
rules.explanation: Account lockout after repeated failed authentication attempts limits online password guessing against local accounts.
rules.impact: Failed-login lockout reduces the effectiveness of brute-force password attacks.

rules.title: Lockout after failed password attempts is configured
rules.explanation: The deny option for faillock denies access after a configured number of consecutive failed authentications within the monitoring interval.
rules.impact: Locking accounts after consecutive failed logon attempts reduces the effectiveness of online brute-force password attacks.

rules.title: Password unlock time is configured
rules.explanation: The unlock_time option defines how many seconds an account remains locked after exceeding the failed-attempt threshold. A value of 0 means the account remains locked until an administrator resets faillock records.
rules.impact: A defined unlock interval sustains the protective effect of lockout and slows repeated brute-force attempts against user accounts.

rules.title: Lockout after failed password attempts includes the root account
rules.explanation: Options such as even_deny_root and root_unlock_time extend faillock behavior to the root account so that repeated failed root authentications also trigger lockout.
rules.impact: Including root in lockout policy reduces the effectiveness of brute-force attacks specifically targeting the privileged account.

rules.title: The number of changed characters in a new password is configured
rules.explanation: The pwquality difok option sets how many characters in a new password must differ from the previous password.
rules.impact: Requiring sufficient character differences prevents trivial password changes that leave accounts vulnerable to reuse of previously observed or compromised passwords.

rules.title: Minimum password length is configured
rules.explanation: The pwquality minlen option sets the minimum allowed length of a new password. Short passwords are significantly easier to guess or crack.
rules.impact: Adequate minimum password length increases the effort required for successful brute-force and guessing attacks.

rules.title: Password complexity is configured
rules.explanation: Password complexity can be enforced using pwquality options such as minclass, dcredit, ucredit, ocredit, and lcredit, which require or credit digits, uppercase, lowercase, and other characters.
rules.impact: Complexity requirements increase password entropy and make guessing and brute-force attacks more difficult.

rules.title: The maximum number of identical consecutive characters in a password is configured
rules.explanation: The pwquality maxrepeat option sets the maximum number of identical consecutive characters permitted in a new password.
rules.impact: Limiting repeated characters reduces use of weak patterns that make passwords easier to guess or crack.

rules.title: The maximum monotonic character sequence length is configured
rules.explanation: The pwquality maxsequence option sets the maximum length of monotonic character sequences (for example 12345 or fedcb) allowed in a new password. A value of 0 disables the check.
rules.impact: Restricting sequential patterns reduces predictable passwords that are easily discovered by guessing and brute-force tools.

rules.title: Password dictionary checking is enabled
rules.explanation: The pwquality dictcheck option determines whether candidate passwords are checked against a cracklib dictionary of common words.
rules.impact: Allowing dictionary words as passwords substantially increases the likelihood of successful guessing and cracking attacks.

rules.title: Password quality checks are enforced for the root user
rules.explanation: When pwquality enforce_for_root is enabled, password quality failures apply even when root changes a password, rather than only displaying a warning.
rules.impact: Enforcing quality for root ensures the most privileged account is not exempt from password-strength policy.

rules.title: Password history is configured
rules.explanation: The pam_pwhistory module stores previous password hashes in /etc/security/opasswd. The remember option defines how many old passwords are retained to prevent reuse.
rules.impact: Password history reduces the chance that users recycle recently used or previously compromised passwords.

rules.title: Password history is enforced for the root user
rules.explanation: When pwhistory enforce_for_root is enabled, password history checks also apply to the root account.
rules.impact: Enforcing history for root reduces reuse of previous privileged passwords that may already be known to an attacker.

rules.title: Pam_pwhistory includes the use_authtok parameter
rules.explanation: The use_authtok option forces pam_pwhistory to use the new password already provided by a preceding stacked password module rather than prompting again.
rules.impact: use_authtok ensures stacked PAM modules evaluate the same candidate password before it is accepted.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include the nullok parameter
