rules.explanation: The nullok argument overrides pam_unix default behavior and permits authentication for accounts with an empty password.
rules.impact: Allowing empty passwords removes a fundamental authentication barrier and enables unauthorized access to accounts without credentials.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include the remember parameter
rules.explanation: The pam_unix remember option stores old passwords using a weaker hashing approach. Password history should instead be managed by pam_pwhistory, which can use the stronger hashing algorithm configured for pam_unix.
rules.impact: Removing remember from pam_unix ensures historical password hashes are stored with a strong algorithm, increasing the effort required to recover old passwords from /etc/security/opasswd.

rules.title: Pam_unix uses a strong password hashing algorithm
rules.explanation: Password hashing performs a one-way transformation of a password into a stored digest. pam_unix should be configured to use a strong algorithm such as SHA-512 or yescrypt.
rules.impact: Stronger hashes increase the computational effort required for an attacker to recover local user passwords from stolen hash data.

rules.title: Pam_unix includes the use_authtok parameter
rules.explanation: The use_authtok option forces pam_unix to set the new password to the value already provided by a preceding stacked password module.
rules.impact: use_authtok allows multiple PAM modules to validate the same new password before it is committed.

rules.title: Maximum password lifetime is configured
rules.explanation: PASS_MAX_DAYS in /etc/login.defs sets the maximum number of days a password may be used before it must be changed.
rules.impact: Without expiration, a compromised password can provide long-term access with no automatic revocation through normal password aging.

rules.title: Minimum password lifetime is configured
rules.explanation: PASS_MIN_DAYS in /etc/login.defs defines the minimum number of days that must elapse before a password can be changed again. A value of 0 disables the restriction.
rules.impact: A minimum lifetime helps prevent users from cycling through passwords rapidly to defeat password-history controls and return to a preferred, potentially compromised password.

rules.title: Password expiration warning days are configured
rules.explanation: PASS_WARN_AGE defines how many days before password expiration users receive a warning, allowing planned password changes.
rules.impact: Without adequate warning, unexpected expirations can lock users out and encourage insecure recovery practices.

rules.title: A strong password hashing algorithm is configured
rules.explanation: ENCRYPT_METHOD in /etc/login.defs selects the hashing algorithm used for new account passwords. Yescrypt or SHA-512 provide strong protection.
rules.impact: Weak algorithms such as MD5 or DES allow rapid offline cracking if the password database is disclosed.

rules.title: Inactive password lockout is configured
rules.explanation: INACTIVE in user aging configuration defines how many days after password expiration an account is locked. A modest value deactivates abandoned accounts.
rules.impact: Accounts with expired passwords that are never locked remain available with stale credentials and are a common unauthorized-access vector.

rules.title: The last password change date is not in the future
rules.explanation: The last password change date recorded for each user must not be in the future, which can indicate manipulation of /etc/shadow to bypass aging policy.
rules.impact: A future password-change date can prevent forced password rotation and is a strong indicator of unauthorized shadow-file modification.

rules.title: Root is the only UID 0 account
rules.explanation: UID 0 grants full superuser privileges. Only the root account should have UID 0.
rules.impact: Additional UID 0 accounts provide equivalent root access while bypassing normal monitoring expectations and are a classic backdoor technique.

rules.title: Root is the only account with GID 0
rules.explanation: GID 0 is the primary group ID associated with the root group. Ordinary user accounts should not use GID 0 as their primary group.
rules.impact: Accounts with primary GID 0 can inherit privileged group rights and increase the risk of unintended privilege escalation.

rules.title: Root is the only group with GID 0
rules.explanation: Only the root group should be assigned GID 0 in the group database.
rules.impact: Additional groups with GID 0 can grant unauthorized privileged access to system resources.

rules.title: The root password is set
rules.explanation: The root account should have a password configured so that privileged local authentication is not left unset.
rules.impact: An unset root password leaves a critical authentication gap for privileged access.

rules.title: Root PATH integrity is configured
rules.explanation: The root user PATH must not contain the current directory (.) or empty elements. Directories in PATH should be owned by root and not writable by other users.
rules.impact: A writable or relative PATH entry allows placement of malicious binaries that execute in place of system commands when run as root.

rules.title: The root user umask is configured
rules.explanation: The root umask determines default permission bits cleared on newly created files and directories. A restrictive value such as 027 or 077 is appropriate for privileged accounts.
rules.impact: A permissive root umask can cause newly created privileged files to be readable or writable by unintended users.
rules.scope: Files /etc/profile, /etc/bashrc, or the root user shell settings.

rules.title: System accounts do not have a valid login shell
rules.explanation: System accounts such as bin and daemon should use a non-login shell (for example /usr/sbin/nologin) rather than an interactive shell such as /bin/bash.
rules.impact: Interactive shells on system accounts increase the chance those accounts can be used for interactive logon if credentials are obtained.

rules.title: Accounts without a valid login shell are locked
rules.explanation: Accounts configured with a non-login shell should also be locked so they cannot authenticate through services that do not honor the shell restriction alone.
rules.impact: Unlocked non-login accounts may still be usable for some authentication paths, creating unexpected access opportunities.

rules.title: Nologin is not listed in /etc/shells
rules.explanation: The /etc/shells file lists shells considered valid for user login. Paths such as /sbin/nologin or /usr/sbin/nologin should not appear in this list.
rules.impact: Listing nologin in /etc/shells can cause some services to treat it as a valid interactive shell, weakening account lockdown.

rules.title: The default user shell timeout is configured
rules.explanation: The TMOUT variable sets the idle time after which an interactive shell session is terminated. A value of 900 seconds or less is commonly required.
rules.impact: Without a shell timeout, abandoned sessions remain active and can be abused by anyone who gains access to the terminal or hijacks the session.

rules.title: The default user umask is configured
rules.explanation: A default umask of 027 or 077 in global shell profiles ensures newly created files are not accessible to unrelated users by default.
rules.impact: A permissive default umask (for example 022) can cause scripts, configuration files, and data to be world-readable and disclose sensitive information.

rules.title: The default user umask in /etc/profile.d is configured
rules.explanation: Drop-in scripts under /etc/profile.d can set the default umask for interactive user sessions. These settings should enforce a restrictive default.
rules.impact: Misconfigured profile.d umask settings can leave newly created user files overly accessible to other local accounts.

rules.title: The journald service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: systemd-journald collects and stores system log data, including security and authentication events, for local review and forwarding.
rules.impact: Without a running journald, many system and security events are not collected, impairing detection and investigation.

rules.title: The rsyslog service is enabled
rules.explanation: When rsyslog is used for system logging, the service should be enabled so that it starts at boot and continues to record events.
rules.impact: If rsyslog is not enabled at boot, logging events may not be recorded after restart until the service is started manually.

rules.title: Default rsyslog file permissions are configured
rules.explanation: rsyslog creates log files that do not yet exist. Default file-creation permissions determine who can read newly created logs.
rules.impact: Overly permissive default log permissions can expose sensitive operational and security data to unauthorized local users.

rules.title: Only one logging system is in use
rules.explanation: Concurrent use of multiple logging systems without clear coordination can duplicate or omit events. The system should operate with a single coherent logging design.
rules.impact: Conflicting logging configurations can create incomplete trails and blind spots during incident investigation.

rules.title: Journald compression is configured
rules.explanation: journald can compress stored journal data to reduce disk consumption and extend practical retention of historical logs.
rules.impact: Without compression, journals consume more space and may rotate away evidence needed for retrospective incident analysis.

rules.title: Journald log rotation is configured
rules.explanation: journald rotation settings control how journal files are overwritten or vacated as they grow, preventing uncontrolled disk consumption.
rules.impact: Unconfigured rotation can fill disks or cause abrupt loss of older logs when storage is exhausted.

rules.title: Access to journald log files is configured
rules.explanation: Permissions on journald log files and directories should restrict read access to authorized administrative users and groups.
rules.impact: Overly permissive journal access can disclose authentication events, security configuration details, and operational information to unauthorized local users.
rules.scope: Log files in /var/log/journal/ and settings in /etc/systemd/journald.conf.

rules.title: The rsyslog package is installed
rules.explanation: rsyslog is a system logging daemon that collects, filters, and stores log messages and can forward them to remote collectors.
rules.impact: Without a configured system logger, traditional syslog-based event collection and centralized forwarding capabilities are unavailable.

rules.title: Journald ForwardToSyslog is disabled when not required
rules.explanation: When journald is the primary logging system, ForwardToSyslog should be disabled unless logs must also be handed off to a syslog daemon.
rules.impact: Unnecessary ForwardToSyslog can duplicate events across logging systems, inflate storage, and complicate correlation during investigations.

rules.title: Journald compression is configured
rules.explanation: journald compression reduces the disk footprint of stored journals and supports longer retention of historical events.
rules.impact: Uncompressed journals rotate sooner under space pressure, increasing the chance that older security events are lost before review.

rules.title: Persistent journald storage is configured
rules.explanation: The Storage=persistent setting causes journald to write logs under /var/log/journal so that journals survive reboot. Without persistent storage, journals may be kept only in volatile memory.
rules.impact: Volatile-only journals are lost on reboot, destroying security evidence that preceded a crash or attacker-induced restart.

rules.title: Rsyslog logging is configured
rules.explanation: The files /etc/rsyslog.conf and /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf define logging rules and the destination files used for classes of messages.
rules.impact: A large amount of security-relevant information is processed through rsyslog; incomplete configuration can omit critical events from local logs.

rules.title: Rsyslog is configured to send logs to a remote host
rules.explanation: rsyslog can forward collected events to a remote logging host, supporting centralized log management and off-host retention.
rules.impact: Remote log storage protects integrity against local attackers who obtain root and attempt to alter or delete on-host logs.

rules.title: Rsyslog is not configured to receive remote logs
rules.explanation: Unless the host is a designated central log collector, rsyslog should not accept inbound logs over the network via modules such as imtcp or imudp.
rules.impact: Accepting remote logs opens network listeners that can be abused to inject forged records or exhaust disk space.

rules.title: Logrotate is configured for system logs
rules.explanation: logrotate, configured through /etc/logrotate.conf and /etc/logrotate.d/, rotates and retains system log files according to size or age policies.
rules.impact: Without rotation, log growth can exhaust disk space and disrupt services while also impairing long-term log manageability.

rules.title: Rsyslog-gnutls is installed
rules.explanation: The rsyslog-gnutls package provides TLS streaming support for encrypting syslog traffic when forwarding logs.
rules.impact: Without TLS support, log forwarding may occur in cleartext and expose sensitive event data on the network.

rules.title: Rsyslog forwarding uses gtls
rules.explanation: rsyslog forwarding configuration should use TLS (for example via omfwd with StreamDriver="gtls") when sending logs to remote collectors.
rules.impact: Cleartext log forwarding allows interception of security events in transit and reduces trust in centralized logging.

rules.title: CA certificates for rsyslog TLS are configured
rules.explanation: A certificate authority (CA) trust configuration is used by rsyslog to validate remote TLS logging servers during encrypted forwarding.
rules.impact: Without CA validation, an rsyslog client may trust a rogue collector and send logs to an attacker-controlled endpoint.

rules.title: Rsyslog is installed
rules.explanation: rsyslog is an enhanced syslog implementation with filtering, formatting, and remote forwarding capabilities. When syslog-style logging is used, the package must be present.
rules.impact: Without rsyslog, traditional syslog collection and SIEM forwarding workflows dependent on it are unavailable.

rules.title: Auditd packages are installed
rules.explanation: auditd provides the userspace component of the Linux audit subsystem, recording security-relevant system calls and events.
rules.impact: Without auditd packages, kernel-level security auditing of privileged operations and sensitive file access cannot be fully implemented.

rules.title: The auditd service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The auditd service should run continuously and be enabled at boot so that kernel audit events are collected without interruption.
rules.impact: A stopped auditd leaves privileged actions, configuration changes, and other security events unrecorded.

rules.title: Auditing of processes that start prior to auditd is enabled
rules.explanation: The kernel parameter audit=1 enables auditing during early boot, before the auditd daemon starts, so initialization events can be captured.
rules.impact: Without early-boot auditing, malicious or anomalous activity during init and early systemd startup may leave no audit trail.

rules.title: The audit backlog limit is sufficient
rules.explanation: audit_backlog_limit sets the kernel audit event queue size. A value of at least 8192 helps prevent event loss under high load before user-space auditd can drain the queue.
rules.impact: A small backlog can drop audit events under load, and attackers may deliberately generate load to conceal actions.

rules.title: Access to log files is configured
rules.explanation: Permissions on system log files should restrict read and write access to authorized administrative users and groups.
rules.impact: Overly permissive log files can disclose sensitive operational and security information to unauthorized local users.
rules.scope: Log files in /var/log/ and their permissions.

rules.title: Audit logs are not deleted automatically
rules.explanation: Settings such as max_log_file_action=keep_logs prevent automatic destruction of old audit logs. Logs should be archived or rotated rather than deleted without retention.
rules.impact: Automatic deletion of audit logs destroys evidence of past incidents and benefits an undetected attacker.

rules.title: The system halts when audit logs are full
rules.explanation: When the audit log partition is full, the system should halt or enter single-user mode rather than continue operating without the ability to record audit events.
rules.impact: Continuing without auditing creates a period in which security events are not recorded; attackers may fill disks deliberately to achieve this state.

rules.title: The system warns when audit log space is low
rules.explanation: space_left_action settings such as email notify administrators when free space on the audit partition approaches a configured threshold.
rules.impact: Without advance warning, audit storage can be exhausted unexpectedly, forcing an abrupt halt or an unaudited operating state.

rules.title: Changes to the system administration scope (sudoers) are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules should record modifications to /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/, which define privileged command authorization policy.
rules.impact: Unaudited sudoers changes can silently expand privileges or introduce NOPASSWD rules that remain undetected until a later review.

rules.title: Actions as another user are always logged
rules.explanation: Auditing identity-changing executions (for example via sudo, su, or runuser) records commands run on behalf of another user and supports attribution during investigations.
rules.impact: Without user-switch auditing, privileged command activity may lack attribution and appear as if performed by a different account.

rules.title: Sudo log file changes are collected
rules.explanation: Modifications to the sudo log file can indicate tampering intended to conceal privileged activity. Auditing those changes helps detect log manipulation.
rules.impact: An attacker with elevated privileges may alter sudo logs to remove evidence; auditing the log file itself helps expose that tampering.

rules.title: Date and time change events are collected
rules.explanation: System calls such as adjtimex, settimeofday, and clock_settime change system time. Auditing them helps detect attempts to manipulate timestamps.
rules.impact: Changing system time can disrupt log correlation and create a false timeline, a common technique for concealing attack activity.

rules.title: Rsyslog logging rules are configured
rules.explanation: The files /etc/rsyslog.conf and /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf define which message classes are recorded and where they are written.
rules.impact: Incomplete rsyslog rules can omit security-relevant messages from local storage and monitoring workflows.

rules.title: Use of privileged commands is collected
rules.explanation: Setuid and setgid programs elevate privileges when executed. Audit rules should track use of these privileged commands.
rules.impact: Without privileged-command auditing, privilege escalation through setuid programs may leave little or no trail.

rules.title: Unsuccessful unauthorized file access attempts are collected
rules.explanation: Auditing failed file-open attempts (for example EACCES and EPERM) helps detect reconnaissance and unauthorized access attempts against protected data.
rules.impact: Repeated access denials are a strong indicator of probing activity that may otherwise go unnoticed.

rules.title: User and group information changes are collected
rules.explanation: Changes to /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/group, and /etc/gshadow record creation, deletion, and modification of accounts and groups.
rules.impact: Unaudited account database edits can hide creation of backdoor accounts, including accounts with elevated privileges.

rules.title: Events that modify /etc/NetworkManager are collected
rules.explanation: The /etc/NetworkManager directory contains NetworkManager configuration files and connection settings that control host networking behavior.
rules.impact: Auditing changes to NetworkManager configuration helps detect unauthorized network reconfiguration that could divert or expose traffic.

rules.title: Successful filesystem mounts are collected
rules.explanation: Auditing successful mount operations tracks attachment of removable media and mounting of network or local filesystems.
rules.impact: Unaudited mounts can conceal introduction of external storage used for data theft or malware staging.

rules.title: Session initiation information is collected
rules.explanation: Auditing session files such as utmp, wtmp, and btmp records login and logout activity used for investigation and detection of unauthorized access.
rules.impact: Without session auditing, an attacker may alter login accounting files to conceal presence on the system.

rules.title: Login and logout events are collected
rules.explanation: Auditing login-related files such as faillog and lastlog records failed authentication attempts and last-login information.
rules.impact: Missing login-event auditing reduces visibility into brute-force attempts and successful unauthorized logons.

rules.title: File deletion events by users are collected
rules.explanation: Auditing unlink, unlinkat, rename, and renameat system calls records deletion and renaming of files by users.
rules.impact: Unaudited deletions can conceal evidence removal, ransomware activity, or intentional data destruction.

rules.title: Events that modify /etc/shadow and /etc/gshadow are collected
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow and /etc/gshadow files store password hashes and related account and group authentication data.
rules.impact: Unexpected modifications may indicate compromise, credential theft preparation, or attempts to conceal account changes.

rules.title: Events that modify /etc/security/opasswd are collected
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/opasswd file stores previous password hashes when password-history PAM modules are in use.
rules.impact: Unauthorized changes to opasswd can undermine password-history controls or indicate tampering with authentication artifacts.

rules.title: Events that modify /etc/nsswitch.conf are collected
rules.explanation: The /etc/nsswitch.conf file configures how the system resolves names and looks up users, groups, and other databases.
rules.impact: Unauthorized nsswitch changes can redirect authentication or name resolution to attacker-controlled sources.

rules.title: Events that modify PAM configuration are collected
rules.explanation: PAM configuration in /etc/pam.conf and /etc/pam.d/ defines authentication stacks for PAM-aware services and applications.
rules.impact: Unaudited PAM changes can weaken authentication requirements or introduce malicious modules without timely detection.

rules.title: Discretionary access control permission modification events are collected
rules.explanation: System calls such as chmod, fchmod, fchmodat, and fchmodat2 change file mode bits that implement discretionary access control.
rules.impact: Auditing permission changes helps detect unauthorized relaxation of file protections that may enable further compromise.

rules.title: Kernel module load and unload events are collected
rules.explanation: Loading and unloading kernel modules through calls such as init_module, finit_module, and delete_module are privileged operations that alter kernel code.
rules.impact: Unaudited module operations can conceal rootkit loading or other unauthorized kernel modifications.

rules.title: The audit configuration is immutable
rules.explanation: Setting the audit configuration to immutable (for example with -e 2) prevents audit rule changes until the next reboot.
rules.impact: Without immutability, an attacker who obtains root can disable auditing or remove rules before performing further malicious actions.

rules.title: Successful filesystem mounts are collected
rules.explanation: Auditing successful mount operations provides visibility into attachment of removable media and mounting of additional filesystems.
rules.impact: Unauthorized mounts without an audit trail can conceal data exfiltration or introduction of malicious content via external storage.

rules.title: Changes to session event files are collected
rules.explanation: Session accounting files record login and logout state. Auditing modifications to these files helps detect tampering with session history.
rules.impact: Monitoring session-related files can alert administrators to unusual logons or attempts to erase evidence of access.

rules.title: Login and logout events are monitored
rules.explanation: Login and logout monitoring records authentication success and failure events used to detect unauthorized access attempts.
rules.impact: Visibility into logon activity supports detection of password guessing and anomalous account use.

rules.title: User file deletion events (unlink) are collected
rules.explanation: Auditing unlink and unlinkat system calls records deletion of files and related attributes by users.
rules.impact: Tracking unprivileged deletion activity can provide evidence of inappropriate removal of protected or sensitive files.

rules.title: User file rename events are collected
rules.explanation: Auditing rename, renameat, and renameat2 system calls records renaming of files and directories by users.
rules.impact: Tracking rename activity helps detect attempts to conceal, relocate, or prepare deletion of sensitive files.

rules.title: Events that modify mandatory access control configuration are collected
rules.explanation: Mandatory access control (MAC) configuration defines confinement policy for processes and objects. Changes to these elements should be recorded by the audit subsystem.
rules.impact: Unaudited MAC policy changes can weaken confinement and allow compromised processes broader access than intended.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful uses of chcon are collected
rules.explanation: The chcon command changes SELinux security contexts on files. Successful and failed uses should be recorded in the audit log.
rules.impact: Auditing chcon helps detect attempts to alter SELinux labels in ways that bypass mandatory access controls.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful uses of setfacl are collected
rules.explanation: The setfacl command modifies filesystem access control lists (ACLs). Successful and failed uses should be recorded in the audit log.
rules.impact: Auditing setfacl helps detect unauthorized expansion or alteration of file access rights beyond standard permission bits.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful uses of chacl are collected
rules.explanation: The chacl command changes POSIX ACLs on files. Successful and failed uses should be recorded in the audit log.
rules.impact: Auditing chacl helps detect unauthorized ACL changes that can expose or alter access to sensitive data.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful uses of usermod are collected
rules.explanation: The usermod command modifies user account attributes such as groups, shell, and UID. Successful and failed uses should be audited.
rules.impact: Auditing usermod is critical for detecting unauthorized account modifications that expand access or establish persistence.

rules.title: Kernel module load and unload events are collected
rules.explanation: Kernel module load and unload operations (init_module, finit_module, delete_module) change running kernel code and should be audited.
rules.impact: Without module auditing, rootkit insertion or removal of security modules may go unnoticed.

rules.title: Kernel module load events (init_module, finit_module) are collected
rules.explanation: The init_module and finit_module system calls load kernel modules into the running kernel.
rules.impact: Auditing module load paths helps detect unauthorized kernel code introduction that could compromise system integrity.

rules.title: Kernel module unload events (delete_module) are collected
rules.explanation: The delete_module system call unloads kernel modules from the running kernel.
rules.impact: Auditing module unload activity helps detect removal of security-relevant modules or other unauthorized kernel changes.

rules.title: The audit configuration is immutable
rules.explanation: Making audit rules immutable until reboot (for example with -e 2) prevents runtime disabling or alteration of the audit policy.
rules.impact: Without immutability, root-level attackers can disable auditing immediately before performing malicious actions.

rules.title: Permissions on audit log files are configured
rules.explanation: auditd log files should have restrictive permissions (commonly no more than 0600) so that only authorized privileged users can read them.
rules.impact: Readable audit logs can disclose security events, configuration details, and user activity patterns useful for planning further attacks.

rules.title: The owner of audit log files is configured
rules.explanation: auditd log files should be owned by root so that only the superuser has full control over audit records.
rules.impact: Audit logs owned by an unprivileged user can be altered or deleted by that user, undermining log integrity as evidence.

rules.title: The group owner of audit log files is configured
rules.explanation: auditd log files should be group-owned by a privileged group such as root so that group membership does not broadly expose audit content.
rules.impact: Audit logs in an overly broad group can disclose privileged activity details to unintended users.

rules.title: Permissions on the audit log directory are configured
rules.explanation: The /var/log/audit directory should have restrictive permissions (for example 0700 or 0750) so that only authorized users can list or access its contents.
rules.impact: Even when individual files are mode 0600, a world-accessible directory can expose metadata such as file names, sizes, and timestamps.

rules.title: Permissions on audit configuration files are configured
rules.explanation: auditd configuration and rules files under /etc/audit should have restrictive permissions (commonly no more than 0640) to prevent unauthorized reading or modification.
rules.impact: Writable audit configuration allows removal or weakening of monitoring rules, a common detection-evasion technique.

rules.title: The owner of audit configuration files is configured
rules.explanation: auditd configuration files should be owned by root to prevent unprivileged users from changing audit policy.
rules.impact: Misowned configuration files can be altered to create blind spots that exclude an attacker's actions from monitoring.

rules.title: The group owner of audit configuration files is configured
rules.explanation: auditd configuration files should be group-owned by a privileged group so that only authorized administrators can modify audit policy.
rules.impact: Configuration files in a broad group allow members to weaken or disable auditing of their own activity.

rules.title: Permissions on audit tools are configured
rules.explanation: Audit utilities such as auditctl, aureport, and ausearch should have restrictive permissions that prevent unauthorized modification of the tools.
rules.impact: Writable audit tools can be replaced with malicious versions that ignore management commands or return forged results.

rules.title: The owner of audit tools is configured
rules.explanation: Audit utilities should be owned by root so that substitution or modification requires superuser privileges.
rules.impact: An audit tool owned by an unprivileged user can be replaced with a malicious version that conceals or falsifies audit administration.

rules.title: The group owner of audit tools is configured
rules.explanation: Audit utilities should be group-owned by a privileged group as part of protecting the audit toolchain from unauthorized modification.
rules.impact: Broad group ownership of audit tools increases the chance of tampering that hides attacker activity from administrators.

rules.title: AIDE is installed
rules.explanation: AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) is a file integrity monitoring system that builds a database of file hashes and attributes to detect unauthorized filesystem changes.
rules.impact: Without integrity monitoring, unauthorized changes to system binaries and configuration files may remain undetected after compromise.

rules.title: Filesystem integrity is checked regularly
rules.explanation: AIDE should run on a regular schedule via cron or a systemd timer so that filesystem integrity deviations are detected promptly.
rules.impact: An installed but unscheduled AIDE deployment may leave unauthorized changes undetected for long periods.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/passwd are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd file lists local user accounts and should be owned by root:root with mode 644 so it is world-readable but writable only by root.
rules.impact: Write access to /etc/passwd allows creation of UID 0 accounts or modification of user shells and home directories, enabling backdoor access.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/passwd- are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd- file is a backup of /etc/passwd and should have permissions no more permissive than the primary file, typically 644 owned by root:root.
rules.impact: A writable passwd backup can be used to restore deleted accounts or alter account data outside normal administrative tools.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/group are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group file defines local groups and membership and should be owned by root:root with mode 644.
rules.impact: Write access to /etc/group allows unauthorized addition of users to privileged groups such as sudo, adm, or disk.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/group- are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group- file is a backup of /etc/group and should have permissions equivalent to the primary group database file.
rules.impact: Compromise of the group backup can restore or inject privileged group membership through backup or recovery paths.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shadow are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow file stores password hashes and should have highly restrictive permissions (for example 000 or 640 with root:shadow ownership).
rules.impact: A readable /etc/shadow exposes password hashes for offline cracking and can lead to widespread credential compromise.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shadow- are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow- file is a backup of /etc/shadow and contains the same sensitive password hash data, requiring equivalent protection.
rules.impact: A weakly protected shadow backup provides an alternate path to obtain password hashes for offline attacks.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/gshadow are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow file stores group passwords and administrator lists and should have restrictive permissions comparable to /etc/shadow.
rules.impact: A readable /etc/gshadow can disclose group passwords and privileged membership information useful for unauthorized group access.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/gshadow- are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow- file is a backup of /etc/gshadow and requires the same restrictive permissions as the primary file.
rules.impact: A more permissive gshadow backup can bypass protections on the primary file and expose group authentication data.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shells are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shells file lists valid login shells and should be owned by root:root with mode 644.
rules.impact: Unauthorized modification of /etc/shells can alter which shells are treated as valid for login and related services.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/security/opasswd are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/opasswd file stores password history hashes and should be owned by root:root with mode 600.
rules.impact: Unauthorized read access to opasswd exposes historical password hashes; write access can undermine password-history enforcement.

rules.title: World-writable files and directories are reviewed
rules.explanation: World-writable files and directories can be modified by any local user. Such objects should have the sticky bit set where appropriate or be remediated.
rules.impact: World-writable locations without proper controls allow any user to overwrite content, enabling malicious replacement of scripts or configurations.

rules.title: No unowned files or directories exist
rules.explanation: Orphaned files lack a valid owning user or group, often because the original account was removed while files remained on disk.
rules.impact: If a deleted UID or GID is later reassigned, the new account inherits access to orphaned files, which may include sensitive data.

rules.title: Accounts in /etc/passwd use shadowed passwords
rules.explanation: Accounts in /etc/passwd should use a shadowed password indicator (x) so that actual password hashes are stored in /etc/shadow rather than in the world-readable passwd file.
rules.impact: Password hashes stored directly in /etc/passwd are readable by any local user and can be attacked offline immediately.

rules.title: Password fields in /etc/shadow are not empty
rules.explanation: An empty password field in /etc/shadow means the account has no password set. Such accounts should be locked or assigned a password.
rules.impact: Accounts with empty shadow password fields may be accessible without authentication through services that permit null passwords.

rules.title: All groups referenced in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group
rules.explanation: Every primary group ID referenced by accounts in /etc/passwd should correspond to a defined group in /etc/group.
rules.impact: Missing group definitions create inconsistent access control and can lead to unexpected permissions or administrative errors.

rules.title: The shadow group is empty
rules.explanation: The shadow group exists so that privileged helper programs can read /etc/shadow. Ordinary users should not be members of this group.
rules.impact: Membership in the shadow group grants read access to password hashes and related aging data that can be used for offline cracking and further account compromise.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist
rules.explanation: Each local user account should have a unique user ID. Duplicate UIDs cause multiple account names to share the same identity for access control.
rules.impact: Users sharing a UID have identical rights to each other's files, which can be abused to obtain another user's data and privileges.

rules.title: No duplicate GIDs exist
rules.explanation: Each local group should have a unique group ID. Duplicate GIDs create ambiguity when evaluating group-based permissions.
rules.impact: Duplicate GIDs can cause distinct groups to share file access rights and may be abused to inherit privileges of another group.

rules.title: No duplicate user names exist
rules.explanation: User names in /etc/passwd must be unique. Duplicate names with different UIDs create ambiguity in authentication and auditing.
rules.impact: Ambiguous user names can cause tools and access policies to apply inconsistently, creating opportunities to bypass intended controls.

rules.title: No duplicate group names exist
rules.explanation: Group names in /etc/group must be unique. Duplicate names with different GIDs create ambiguity when assigning and evaluating group membership.
rules.impact: Ambiguous group names can be handled inconsistently by system tools and may be exploited to obtain unintended group privileges.

rules.title: Local interactive user home directories exist
rules.explanation: Interactive local users should have existing home directories configured and present on the filesystem.
rules.impact: Users without a home directory may create files in unexpected locations such as / or /tmp, increasing the risk of sensitive data placement in system paths.

rules.title: Permissions on local user dot files are configured
rules.explanation: User startup and configuration files such as .bashrc and .profile should have restrictive permissions that prevent other users from modifying them.
rules.impact: Writable dot files allow unauthorized modification of a user's shell environment, which can lead to command injection or credential theft when the user next logs in.
rules.scope: Dot files in user home directories (for example, /home/*/.*).
